title: Imperative and infinitives

objectives.can: Recognise singular and plural imperatives, and negative commands.
Recognise present, perfect and passive infinitives.

explanation.summary: The imperative gives a command to the person addressed, and the infinitive names an action without a person or a number. Both are very short forms, and both are everywhere in the Vulgate: 'Rise', 'Do not be afraid', 'to be able', 'to be baptized'.

sections.heading: The imperative: one stem, one ending
body: The commonest command, the present imperative, is addressed to one person or to several. The singular is the bare stem of the present: the last vowel of the stem is all that is added. The plural adds -te to the stem (with -i- before it in the third conjugation).

So *surge* ('rise!') is singular and *surgite* is plural; *vide* is singular and *videte* plural; *audi* and *audite* likewise. The singular third-conjugation imperative ends in -e (*mitte*, *surge*), and a few very common verbs have lost even that: *dic*, *duc*, *fac*, and the imperative of *fero*. The library holds *dic*, *fac* and *duc*, but not the short imperative of *fero*; it does have *afferte*, the plural of the compound.
A command has a second person only. There is no first or third person imperative, and no passive in the library; the corpus tags every imperative as active.

sections.heading: The future imperative
body: Latin also has a future imperative in -to (singular) and -tote (plural). It is used for commands about the future, for rules and laws, and for a few verbs that have no present imperative, such as *scio* ('know') and *memini* ('remember'): *scitote*, *memento*. The corpus gives these forms the tag Tense=Fut, Mood=Imp.
*esto* and *estote*, from *sum*, are future imperatives that were used in the sense of an ordinary command, 'be'.

sections.heading: Commanding not to
body: A negative command is not made by putting *non* before the imperative. The ordinary way in the Vulgate is *noli* (singular) or *nolite* (plural), which are the imperative of *nolo*, 'be unwilling', followed by an infinitive: *nolite timere* is 'do not fear', literally 'be unwilling to fear'.

Two other ways are met. One is *ne* with the present subjunctive: *Ne timeas*, 'do not fear', where the subjunctive is learned in a later stage. The other is *non* with the future indicative, a command in the form of a statement, as in *Non occides*, 'you shall not kill'. The Vulgate uses it for the commandments, following the Hebrew.

sections.heading: The infinitive
body: The infinitive is the verb's name form: it has tense and voice but no person and no number. In English it is 'to do'. It is used after verbs such as *possum*, *volo*, *nolo* and *debeo* (the complementary infinitive), as the subject of a short sentence, and in indirect statement, which comes later.

The present active infinitive ends in -re: -are, -ere, -ere, -ire in the four conjugations. The present passive ends in -ri, with the third conjugation shortening to -i (*baptizari*, *tentari*, but *dimitti*). The perfect active ends in -isse, added to the perfect stem: *vidisse*, *fecisse*.

sections.heading: Passive perfect and shortened forms
body: The perfect passive infinitive has two words, like the perfect passive tense: the perfect participle and *esse*. It is the participle of the last lesson plus the infinitive of *sum*, and the participle agrees with the subject of the infinitive. The corpus gives the participle its own tag, so these two-word infinitives are best recognised by eye: a participle followed by *esse*.

Some perfect infinitives are shortened. *nosse*, 'to know', is the old perfect of *nosco* (originally 'to have come to know') and is the form the Vulgate prefers to the longer one. Read it as a present in sense.

misunderstandings: *noli* and *nolite* are not forms of a verb 'to be unwilling' meaning 'not': they are real commands, 'be unwilling', and need an infinitive. *noli* is singular, *nolite* is plural.
The infinitive is not the tense of a command. *surge* is a command; *surgere* is only 'to rise'.

A form ending in -i is not always a passive infinitive. In the third conjugation -i may be the present passive infinitive (*dimitti*), the fourth-conjugation singular imperative (*audi*), or something else. Only the context settles it, and the exercises use only words the analyser read with a single reading.
A form in -re is not always an active infinitive. It can also be a second singular passive in older Latin; the analyser is unsure of many such forms, which is why the library offers few of them.

Some forms that look passive are not. *loqui* and other deponent infinitives, and *fieri*, are passive in form but active in meaning; the library tags them as active, and they are taught in a later lesson. The exercises here draw on ordinary verbs only.

deeper.heading: Which infinitives the library can test
body: The analysis is automatic. Many forms in -re and -ri are read by the analyser in more than one way and are therefore not used for exercises. The present active infinitives that survive are largely those of compounds of *eo* and *fero* (*transire*, *exire*, *offerre*, *inferre*) and of deponent verbs. This is a limit of the tools, not a rule of Latin.
